content: The study identified a significant overall effect of exercise compared to the control group after the intervention period. The participants in the study ranged in age from 18 to 65 years. The exercise interventions lasted between 6 and 16 weeks, with sessions lasting 20 to 60 minutes, performed 3 to 5 times per week. Eight studies reported statistically significant improvements in VO2 max or VO2 peak in the intervention group after training, while two studies found no significant improvement in these outcomes. Additionally, two trials reported a significant increase in the mean forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) in the intervention group compared to the control group. Farinatti (2010) observed a significant improvement in the slope and intercept values for the rate-workload relationship. Thirteen studies reported statistically significant improvements in cardiopulmonary-related parameters, while two studies did not find significant improvements in the intervention group. Meta-analysis results revealed a significant change in VO2 max between the intervention and control groups, favoring the intervention. There was a trend toward increased VO2 max in participants undergoing aerobic and resistance exercise compared to those engaging in normal activities in the control group. O’Brien (2016) downgraded the evidence for VO2 max to very low due to high attrition rates (withdrawals >15%), suspected publication bias, substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 67%), and the lower confidence interval not crossing the estimated clinically important change in VO2 max. HR max was downgraded to moderate due to attrition and performance bias. Exercise time was also downgraded to moderate for similar reasons but later upgraded to high due to a clear dose-response relationship. Strength outcomes were downgraded from high to low due to incomplete outcome data (withdrawals >15%), suspected publication bias, and moderate-to-considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 46% and 88% for chest press and leg press, respectively). O’Brien (2010) rated VO2 max as moderate due to heterogeneity in the included studies but later upgraded it to high due to a dose-response relationship. Maximum heart rate (HR max) and exercise time were rated as high, with no reason for downgrading. Strength outcomes were downgraded to low due to a higher magnitude of indirectness. O’Brien (2004) downgraded the evidence to low due to potential publication bias, attrition bias (20% dropout in six studies and >50% dropout in two studies), and the small number of trials and participants. Heterogeneity may have occurred due to the variety of exercise interventions used. This low GRADE was later upgraded to high due to evidence of a dose-response relationship. O’Brien (2008) downgraded the evidence to low due to significant variation among individual studies in the types of interventions, participants, and outcomes, which may have led to heterogeneity and indirectness. There was also a risk of attrition bias due to high withdrawal rates (>15%) and a lack of blinding to the pre-intervention, potentially resulting in the Hawthorne effect. Performance bias was also suspected due to increased interaction between investigators and participants in the exercise group, leading to more favorable outcomes for exercisers compared to non-exercisers. The review included a small number of studies (n = 10), and total outcome data were unavailable for 69 participants (17%). This was later upgraded to high due to evidence of a dose-response relationship. Nixon (2005) downgraded the evidence to low due to a high risk of attrition bias (withdrawal rates ranging from 4% to 76%) and indirectness caused by heterogeneity in outcome measures. This was later upgraded to high due to evidence of a dose-response relationship. Pedro (2017) downgraded the evidence to moderate due to indirectness, which might have been caused by differences in the types of individuals, exercise interventions, and assessment methods across studies. Serious inconsistency in findings was also noted. Chaparro (2018) rated the evidence as low due to publication bias and indirectness caused by differences among the included studies. This was later upgraded to high due to the presence of a dose-response relationship. Gomes Neto (2015) rated the evidence as moderate due to the risk of bias, as the risk of selective reporting was uncertain, and none of the studies described blinding of therapists. This was later upgraded to high due to the presence of a dose-response relationship. Zech (2019) downgraded the evidence to moderate because nine of the 27 included studies showed a high risk of bias and potential publication bias. Poton (2017) downgraded the evidence to moderate due to risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision, as there was insufficient information in the review. Voigt (2018) downgraded the evidence to moderate due to heterogeneity resulting from different exercise interventions and small sample sizes. This was later upgraded to high due to the presence of a dose-response relationship. Ibeneme (2019a) downgraded the evidence to moderate due to risk of bias, inconsistency in outcome measures, and variability in the types of interventions used in the study. This was later upgraded to high due to the presence of a dose-response relationship. Regarding the effects of physical activity on cardiometabolic markers among people living with HIV (PLWH), aerobic training resulted in reductions in total cholesterol in two studies and LDL cholesterol in one study, while another study showed no decrease in total cholesterol under controlled dietary conditions. Concurrent training led to a drop in total cholesterol in one study. Triglyceride levels improved after resistance training, and free fatty acids decreased, while HDL cholesterol increased after either aerobic or resistance training. No effect was observed on HOMA or insulin concentrations by any exercise modality. Glucose levels reduced after aerobic training in one study. Body fat percentage decreased in response to all forms of training except in one study, although the methods of assessment were poor in most studies. Only one study assessed inflammatory markers, showing decreases in hs-CRP, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-18 after aerobic training, with only IL-18 decreasing after resistance training. No effect on CD4 count was observed, indicating the safety of training in this population. Aerobic and concurrent training improved VO2 max, while resistance training reduced fat mass and improved muscle strength. However, there is no true consensus or sufficient evidence to support the improvement of inflammatory and lipid profiles. Aerobic and resistance training were effective in improving BMI, fat mass percentage, and waist-to-hip ratio, while resistance training increased body weight and muscle strength and was slightly better at reducing fat mass. Concurrent exercise studies were inconclusive. Aerobic training had a small advantage over resistance training in reducing total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol in one study. Few studies examined blood lipids, glucose, and bone density, which are important factors in participants with chronic HIV and HAART. Overall, exercise appears to benefit the metabolic profile of PLWH.
